tagline: A hunter with a secret red searchlight
summary: A slender black dragonfish that shines red light from an organ beneath each eye—a colour almost no other deep-sea animal can see. Its own eyes are tuned to red, giving it a private beam for spotting prey that never knows it is lit.

stats.depth: About 500–3,900 m; thought to stay below 500 m
stats.range: All oceans, from about 66°N to about 30°S; not known from the Mediterranean

facts.title: Two kinds of light
facts.text: Like most deep-sea animals it has a blue light organ, just behind the eye. But a large organ beneath the eye glows far-red—the 'stoplight' that gives the fish its name.

facts.title: A private waveband
facts.text: Red light barely travels in seawater, so nearly all deep-sea animals have lost the ability to see it. A red beam may let the loosejaw illuminate prey and signal to its own kind without being noticed.

facts.title: Borrowed pigment for red vision
facts.text: Unusually, its retina holds a pigment derived from bacteriochlorophyll (a bacterial cousin of chlorophyll) that boosts sensitivity to red light. Its similarity to pigments in copepods the fish eats suggests a dietary origin.

facts.title: Where the pigment comes from
facts.text: A 2016 study looked for bacteria in the eye that might make the pigment and found none; the chemical was spread throughout the retina, and its origin remains unclear.

facts.title: A hinged head
facts.text: A flexible joint between the back of the skull and the first vertebra lets it tip its head far back, widening its gape to swallow large prey.

references.title: Douglas, R.H., Mullineaux, C.W. & Partridge, J.C. (2000). Long-wave sensitivity in deep-sea stomiid dragonfish with far-red bioluminescence: evidence for a dietary origin of the chlorophyll-derived retinal photosensitizer of Malacosteus niger. Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 355(1401)
references.publisher: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B (PubMed Central)

references.title: Douglas, R.H. et al. (2016). Localisation and origin of the bacteriochlorophyll-derived photosensitizer in the retina of the deep-sea dragon fish Malacosteus niger. Scientific Reports 6: 39395

image.alt: A long, slender, glossy black fish lying on a blue tray, its long lower jaw hanging open and a bright red spot below its eye.
image.caption: A stoplight loosejaw trawled from about 1,500 m; the red spot under the eye is its red light organ.
image.creator: NOAA Northeast Fisheries Science Center
